concepts.title: Diffusion Model
concepts.one_liner: Diffusion models are a class of generative models that learn to create data by reversing a signal corruption process.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models are a class of model that uses a strategy of breaking a complex task into many simple pieces. Unlike autoregressive models that remove pixels one by one, diffusion models use a signal corruption process. Starting with an uncorrupted image $\mathbf{x}_0$, they add noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ to result in a noisy version $\mathbf{x}_1$. This process is repeated, adding noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to produce an even noisier signal $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on. Most commonly, the noise used is isotropic Gaussian noise.

(see figure: An autoregressive sequence in reverse is a corruption process that removes one pixel at a time.)

(see figure: Forward diffusion process.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generating complex structured data like images directly from noise is difficult. Diffusion models solve this by breaking the generation task into a sequence of small, manageable denoising steps, using a controlled corruption process to create the necessary training data.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models generate data by iteratively reversing a multi-step corruption process.

Diffusion models instead use the following corruption process: starting with an uncorrupted image, $\mathbf{x}_0$, they add noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ to this image, resulting in a noisy version of the image, $\mathbf{x}_1$. Then they repeat this process, adding noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_1$ to produce an even noisier signal $\mathbf{x}_2$, and so on.

concepts.title: Forward Diffusion Process
concepts.one_liner: The forward diffusion process iteratively adds noise to an image until it becomes indistinguishable from pure Gaussian noise.
concepts.content:
The forward diffusion process is a signal corruption method where, starting with an uncorrupted image $\mathbf{x}_0$, noise $\mathbf{\epsilon}_0$ is added to produce a noisy version $\mathbf{x}_1$. This is repeated to produce increasingly noisier signals $\mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_T$. Most commonly, isotropic Gaussian noise is used.

(see figure: Forward diffusion process.)

After $T$ steps, the image $\mathbf{x}_T$ looks like pure noise if $T$ is large enough. Specifically, if the following noise process is used, then $\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$ as $T \rightarrow \infty$:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_t &= \sqrt{(1-\beta_t)}\mathbf{x}_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\mathbf{\epsilon}_t\\ \epsilon_t &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) \end{aligned}$$
The $\beta_t$ values are typically $\leq 1$ and can be fixed for all $t$ or set according to a schedule that changes the amount of noise added over time.
concepts.motivation_md: This process provides a systematic way to transform structured data into noise, which serves as the foundation for creating training examples for the reverse (generative) process.
concepts.recap_md: - Forward diffusion transforms data into noise by adding Gaussian noise at each step $t$.

concepts.title: Reverse Diffusion Process
concepts.one_liner: The reverse diffusion process uses a trained neural network to iteratively remove noise and recover a clean image from a noisy signal.
concepts.content:
Diffusion models train a neural net $f_{\theta}$ to reverse the corruption process. This is achieved via supervised learning on sequences of images that get progressively noisier. By flipping these sequences in time, we obtain training examples for the mapping $\mathbf{x}_t \rightarrow \mathbf{x}_{t-1}$, which are then fit by the predictor $f_{\theta}$.

(see figure: Reverse diffusion process. The forward process creates supervision to train the reverse process.)

The model $f_{\theta}$ acts as a denoiser that learns to remove a small amount of noise. When applied repeatedly starting from pure noise, the process coalesces into a noise-less image resembling the training data. Training involves two main steps:
1. Generate training data by corrupting images (forward process).
2. Train a neural net to invert each corruption step (reverse process).
concepts.motivation_md: While turning data into noise is easy, turning noise into data is hard. This process enables generation by learning to perform the difficult task of denoising in small, incremental steps.
concepts.recap_md: - The reverse process uses a neural network to map a noisy image $\mathbf{x}_t$ back to a cleaner version $\mathbf{x}_{t-1}$.

concepts.title: Denoiser
concepts.one_liner: A denoiser is a neural network trained to remove a small amount of noise from an image.
concepts.content: A denoiser, denoted as $f_{\theta}$, is a neural network that learns to remove a little bit of noise from an image. If this denoiser is applied over and over, starting with pure noise, the process should coalesce on a noise-less image that looks like one of the training examples.
concepts.motivation_md: The denoiser is the core functional component of a diffusion model, responsible for the actual generation of structured data from noise.
concepts.recap_md: - A denoiser $f_{\theta}$ performs the mapping from a noisy state to a less noisy state.

concepts.title: Training Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Training diffusion models involves teaching a neural network to predict either the less noisy image or the noise itself at specific time steps.
concepts.content:
To improve predictions, the denoising function can observe the time step $t$ as an input: $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$. Knowing $t$ helps the denoiser distinguish between a corrupted scene (likely at large $t$) and a naturally chaotic texture (likely at small $t$).

(see figure: Training a diffusion model consists of first producing training pairs of the form {noisy image, less noisy image}. Then do supervised learning on these pairs.)

The denoiser is trained using a loss $\mathcal{L}$, such as $L_2$ distance. While some models output Gaussian density parameters for probabilistic interpretations, others use various prediction models for $f_{\theta}$. A common reparameterization trick is to train the model to predict the noise $\epsilon_t$ rather than the signal:
$$\begin{aligned} f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_t, t) &= \epsilon_t \\ \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t-1} &= \mathbf{x}_t + \epsilon_t \end{aligned}$$
Ultimately, diffusion models turn images into noise to create training sequences for a process that turns noise back into data.
concepts.motivation_md: Providing the time step $t$ and reparameterizing the model to predict noise are techniques that make the optimization problem easier and more stable for the neural network.
concepts.recap_md: - Training uses pairs of {noisy image, less noisy image} generated by the forward process.

concepts.title: Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)
concepts.one_liner: A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) is a system that synthesizes data in a single step using a generator and a discriminator.
concepts.content: A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a model that attempts to directly output samples from a complex distribution in one step. The core idea is that synthetic data looks like real data if a classifier cannot distinguish between them. GANs consist of two neural networks: the generator, $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, which synthesizes data from noise, and a discriminator, $d_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^1$, which tries to classify between synthesized and real data.
concepts.motivation_md: GANs were designed to generate high-quality samples in a single forward pass, avoiding the iterative sampling required by autoregressive or diffusion models.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs use a competitive framework between a generator and a discriminator.

concepts.title: Generator
concepts.one_liner: A generator is a function that produces a synthetic output, such as an image, by mapping a randomized input vector and an optional label to the output space.
concepts.content:
One way to make a function stochastic is to make it a deterministic function of a stochastic input. We define $g$ as a function, called a **generator**, that takes a randomized vector $\mathbf{z}$ as input along with the label/description $\mathbf{y}$, and produces an image $\mathbf{x}$ as output, that is, $g: \mathcal{Z} \times \mathcal{Y} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$. Then this function can output a different image $\mathbf{x}$ for each different setting of $\mathbf{z}$. The generative process is as follows. First sample $\mathbf{z}$ from a prior $p(Z)$, then deterministically generate an image based on $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{y}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} \sim p(Z)\\
    \mathbf{x} = g(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{y})
\end{aligned}
$$

Graphical model for generating $X \| Y, Z$.

[FIGURE:b59cceb106ac5b5a]

This procedure is shown in @fig-generative_models-image_generation_with_z:

(see figure: Making a generator stochastic by conditioning on a random variable.)
concepts.motivation_md: Generators allow us to model complex, high-dimensional probability distributions (like the space of all natural images) by transforming simple, well-understood noise distributions through a deterministic function.

concepts.title: Latent Variables
concepts.one_liner: Latent variables are unobserved inputs to a generator that specify attributes of the output not determined by the explicit label.
concepts.content: Usually we draw $\mathbf{z}$ from a simple distribution such as Gaussian noise, that is, $p(Z) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1})$. The way to think of $\mathbf{z}$ is that it is a vector of **latent variables**, which specify all the attributes of the images other than those determined by the label. These variables are called latent because they are not directly observed in the training data (it just consists of images $\mathbf{x}$ and their labels $\mathbf{y}$). In our example, $\mathbf{y}$ tells $g$ to make a bird but the $\mathbf{z}$-vector is what specifies exactly which bird. Different dimensions of $\mathbf{z}$ specify different attributes, such as the size, color, pose, background, and so on; everything necessary to fully determine the output image.
concepts.motivation_md: Latent variables provide a way to capture the underlying factors of variation in data that aren't explicitly labeled, allowing a model to generate diverse outputs for the same class.

concepts.title: Sampling from a Generative Model
concepts.one_liner: Sampling is the process of querying a learned generator with new, randomized latent vectors to produce novel outputs.
concepts.content:
How can we learn to synthesize images that look realistic? The machine learning way to do this is to start with a training set of *examples* of real images, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Recall that in supervised learning, an *example* was defined as an {`input`, `output`} pair; here things are actually no different, only the `input` happens to be the null set. We feed these examples to a learner, which spits out a generator function. Later, we may query the generator with new, randomized $\mathbf{z}$-vectors to produce novel outputs, a process called **sampling** from the model. (see figure: Learning and using a generator.)
concepts.motivation_md: Sampling allows us to use a trained model to create new, never-before-seen data points that share the characteristics of the training set.

concepts.title: Objective of Generative Modeling
concepts.one_liner: The goal of generative modeling is to create a generator that produces synthetic data identically distributed to the true training data.
concepts.content:
The objective of the learner is to create a generator that produces *synthetic* data, $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, that looks like the *real* data, $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. There are a lot of ways of define "looks like" and they each result in a different kind of generative model. Two examples are:

1. Synthetic data looks like real data if matches the real data in terms of certain marginal statistics, for example, it has the same mean color as real photos, or the same color variance, or the same edge statistics.

2. Synthetic data looks like real data if it has high probability under a density model fit to the real data.

The first approach works well when we only want to match certain properties of the training data. The second approach is better when we want to produce synthetic data that matches *all* statistics of the training examples. In practice, we may not be able to match all statistics, due to limits of the model's capacity. concepts.title: Generalization vs. Memorization in Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: A good generative model must generalize by producing novel samples that look real without simply memorizing the training data.
concepts.content: What if our model just memorizes all the training examples and generates random draws from this memory? Indeed, memorized training samples perfectly satisfy the goal of making synthetic data that looks real. A second, sometimes overlooked, property of a good generative model is that it be a simple, or smooth, function, so that it generalizes to producing synthetic samples that look like the training data but are not identical to it. A generator that only regurgitates the training data is overfit in the same way a classifier that memorizes the training data is overfit. In both cases, the true goal is to fit the training data and to do so with a function that generalizes.

concepts.title: Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Generative models that produce a probability density function fit to training data to estimate data likelihood or guide sample generation.
concepts.content:
Some generative models not only produce generators but also yield a probability density function $p_{	heta}$, fit to the training data. This density function may play a role in training the generator (e.g., we want the generator to produce samples from $p_{	heta}$), or the density function may be the goal itself (e.g., we want to be able to estimate the probability of datapoints in order to detect anomalies).

(see figure: The indirect approach to generative modeling. The scoring function can be either a probability density or an energy function. The models we learned about in @sec-stat_image_models.)

In fact, some generative models *only* produce a density $p_{	heta}$ and do not learn any explicit generator function. Instead, samples can be drawn from $p_{	heta}$ using a sampling algorithm, such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), that takes a density as input and produces samples from it as output. This is a form of the indirect approach to synthesizing data.
concepts.motivation_md: Density models are essential when we need to quantify how likely a specific data point is. This is useful for anomaly detection, where we identify low-probability outliers, or for providing a formal mathematical objective to train a generator that mimics a training distribution.

concepts.title: Divergence between Distributions
concepts.one_liner: A measure of closeness between two probability distributions used as an optimization objective for density models.
concepts.content:
The objective of the learner for a density model is to output a density function $p_{\theta}$ that is as close as possible to $p_{\texttt{data}}$. We measure this closeness by defining a divergence $D$ between the two distributions and solving the optimization problem:
$$\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} D(p_{\theta}, p_{\texttt{data}})$$
Because we only have samples $\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ rather than the true function $p_{\texttt{data}}$, we require a divergence that can be calculated using only these samples. A divergence need not be a proper distance metric; it can be nonsymmetric ($D(p,q) \neq D(q,p)$) and does not need to satisfy the triangle inequality. It is defined by two properties: nonnegativity and $D(p,q) = 0 \iff p=q$.
concepts.motivation_md: To train a model to match a target distribution, we need a way to quantify 'error' or distance between the model's distribution and the true data distribution. Divergence provides this mathematical objective.

concepts.title: Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence
concepts.one_liner: A common divergence measure that leads to the maximum likelihood estimate of a model's parameters.
concepts.content:
The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is a common choice for measuring the distance between distributions. Minimizing the forward KL divergence $\mathrm{KL}(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta)$ is equivalent to maximizing the expected log likelihood of the training data under the model's density function:
$$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}^* &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{p_\theta} \mathrm{KL}\left(p_{\text {data }} \| p_\theta\right) \\ &= \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}\big[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\big] \\ &\approx \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{p_\theta} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$
The forward KL divergence measures the probability of the data under the model distribution. In contrast, the reverse KL divergence, $\mathrm{KL}(p_\theta \| p_{\text {data }})$, measures the probability of the model's samples under the data distribution; this is usually uncomputable because the true data distribution is unknown.
concepts.motivation_md: KL divergence provides a mathematically principled way to derive the Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) objective, which is the standard approach for fitting statistical models to data.

concepts.title: Energy-Based Models (EBMs)
concepts.one_liner: Generative models that learn an unnormalized energy function $E_{\theta}$ instead of a normalized probability density.
concepts.content:
Density models require the constraint $\int_{\mathbf{x}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})d\mathbf{x} = 1$, which is often hard to realize because the normalizing constant $Z(\theta) = \int_{\mathbf{x}} e^{-E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}d\mathbf{x}$ is expensive to compute. Energy-based models (EBMs) address this by learning an unnormalized function $E_{\theta}$. Even without normalization, $E_{\theta}$ can be used for many applications because relative probabilities can be compared:
$$\frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)} = \frac{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_1)}}{e^{-E_\theta(\mathbf{x}_2)}}$$
This is sufficient for sampling via MCMC, outlier detection, and finding the maximum probability datapoint. Furthermore, the gradient of the log probability density with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ is identical to the negative gradient of the energy function:
$$\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) = -\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})$$
Energy functions are insufficient only when true normalized probabilities are required for interpretability or downstream system requirements.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalizing a probability distribution over high-dimensional spaces (like images) is computationally intractable. EBMs bypass this 'partition function' problem by working directly with unnormalized energy scores.

concepts.title: Contrastive Divergence
concepts.one_liner: An optimization technique for energy-based models that contrasts data samples with model samples to approximate the likelihood gradient.
concepts.content:
Contrastive divergence is an optimizer specifically built for maximum likelihood objectives over energy functions. Unlike density models, which implicitly push down density in unobserved regions via normalization, energy functions require an explicit negative term to increase energy where there are no datapoints. On each iteration, the method modifies the energy function to decrease energy for data samples (positive term) and increase energy for samples drawn from the model itself (negative term).

(see figure: Fitting a max likelihood energy function to data, using contrastive divergence. @hinton2002training)

Mathematically, this procedure approximates the gradient of the log likelihood:
$$\nabla_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})] = -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\nabla_{\theta}E_{\theta(\mathbf{x})}] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta} E_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})]$$
By approximating these expectations with samples $\mathbf{x}^{(i)} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} \sim p_{\theta}$, the model is updated to decrease the contrast between data and model samples. When the model perfectly fits the data, the gradient becomes zero.
concepts.motivation_md: Since the normalizing constant $Z(\theta)$ in energy-based models is intractable, we cannot use standard gradient descent on the log-likelihood. Contrastive divergence provides a clever way to approximate that gradient using samples.

concepts.title: Comparing Different Kinds of Generative Models
concepts.one_liner: A categorization of generative models based on whether they provide density/energy functions, explicit generators, or latent variables.
concepts.content:
Generative models can be distinguished by whether they provide density/energy functions, generator functions, or both. Generators typically use latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ to control properties of the generated output. In contrast, density and energy models provide scores related to the likelihood of data, which are useful for anomaly detection or optimization, but they lack latent variables for direct control of samples.

Different families of models offer various trade-offs:
- **Energy-based models**: Provide energy scores; no latents or explicit generator.
- **Autoregressive models**: Provide both density and a generator, but sampling is slow.
- **GANs and VAEs**: Excel at representation learning via low-dimensional latent spaces but do not provide exact densities.
- **Diffusion models**: Use high-dimensional latents and provide a generator, though sampling is slow.

Models can also be categorized by their objectives, hypothesis spaces, and optimization algorithms. For instance, autoregressive models define a hypothesis space, while VAEs refer to a specific conjunction of objective, hypothesis space, and optimizer.
concepts.motivation_md: No single generative model achieves all desirable properties (latent control, exact density estimation, and fast sampling). Understanding these trade-offs is crucial for selecting the right model for a specific task.

Generative models can be distinguished by whether they provide density/energy functions, generator functions, or both. Generators typically use latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ to control properties of the generated output. concepts.title: Gaussian Density Model
concepts.one_liner: The Gaussian distribution is a density model defined by its mean and variance parameters, normalized by a constant to ensure it represents a valid probability distribution.
concepts.content: One of the simplest and most useful density models is the Gaussian distribution, which in one dimension (1D) is: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(x) = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)} \end{aligned}$$ This density has two parameters $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, which are the mean and variance of the distribution. The normalization constant $Z$ ensures that the function is normalized. This is the typical strategy in defining density models: create a parameterized family of functions such that any function in the family is normalized. Given such a family, we search over the parameters to optimize a generative modeling objective.
concepts.motivation_md: Density modeling requires a way to represent the probability of continuous data. The Gaussian distribution provides a mathematically tractable, two-parameter family that can be easily optimized to fit observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - The Gaussian distribution is defined by mean $\theta_1$ and variance $\theta_2$.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood for Gaussian Density Models
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood estimation for a 1D Gaussian density model analytically results in setting the parameters to the empirical mean and variance of the training data.
concepts.content:
For density models, the most common objective is max likelihood: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log p_{\theta}(x)] \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_{\theta}(x^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$ For a 1D Gaussian, this has a simple form: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \log \frac{1}{Z}e^{-(x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2)} = -\log(Z) + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1)^2/(2\theta_2) \end{aligned}$$ Optimizing with respect to $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ could be done via gradient descent or random search, but in this case there is also an analytical solution we can find by setting the gradient to be zero. For $\theta_1^*$ we have: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \big(-\log Z + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)\big)}{\partial \theta_1^*} = 0\\ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)/(2\theta_2^*) = 0\\ \sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)} - \sum_{i=1}^N \theta_1^* = 0\\ \theta_1^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N x^{(i)} \end{aligned}$$ For $\theta_2^*$ we need to note that $Z$ depends on $\theta_2^*$ and in particular notice that $\frac{\partial (-\log Z)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*}$: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \big(-\log Z + \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)\big)}{\partial \theta_2^*} = 0\\ \frac{1}{2\theta_2^*} - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2/(2\theta_2^*)^2 = 0\\ 2\theta_2^* - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N 2(x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2 = 0\\ \theta_2^* = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x^{(i)}-\theta_1^*)^2 \end{aligned}$$ The solutions for $\theta_1^*$ and $\theta_2^*$ are the empirical mean and variance of the data, respectively. To maximize the probability of the data under a Gaussian, we should set the mean and variance of the Gaussian to be the empirical mean and variance of the data.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Model
concepts.one_liner: An autoregressive model generates data sequentially by predicting each new element based on the sequence of elements already generated.
concepts.content:
The idea of an autoregressive model is to synthesize an image pixel by pixel. Each new pixel is decided on based on the sequence already generated. You can think of this as a simple sequence prediction problem: given a sequence of observed pixels, predict the color of the next one. We use the same learned function $f_{\theta}$ to make each subsequent prediction.

(see figure: An autoregressive model, $f_{\theta}$, that generates an image pixel by pixel. The black pixels are the remaining pixels to synthesize. Compare with the Efros-Leung model in @fig-sampling_efros_leung.)

We predict each next pixel from the partial image already completed. The red bordered region is the context the prediction is based on. This context could be the entire image synthesized so far or it could be a smaller region. The green bordered pixel is the one we are predicting given this context. In this example, we always predict the bottom-center pixel in the context window. After making our prediction, we decide what color pixel to add to the image based on that prediction; we may add the color predicted as most likely, or we might sample from the predicted distribution so that we get some randomness in our completion. Then, to predict the next missing pixel we slide the context over by one and repeat.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple density models like single Gaussians are limited. Autoregressive models provide a recipe for building highly expressive models by breaking down complex joint distributions into a sequence of simpler conditional predictions.
concepts.recap_md: - Data is generated one element at a time based on previously generated context.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Prediction as Next-Pixel Classification
concepts.one_liner: Modeling a sequence of pixels can be treated as an inductive process where each next pixel is predicted using a categorical distribution and softmax regression.
concepts.content:
These models can be understood by considering the problem of synthesizing one pixel, then two, and so on. It is straightforward to synthesize a single grayscale pixel, which can take on 256 possible values. A categorical distribution can represent the probability mass function (pmf) over these values. Fitting this distribution to training data involves counting the frequency of each value and normalizing. We can then sample from this distribution to synthesize a random one-pixel image.

To model the distribution over a second grayscale pixel given the first, we model $p(\mathbf{x_2} \bigm | \mathbf{x_1})$. Treating $\mathbf{x}_2$ as a categorical variable, we can use softmax regression, similar to image classification but modeling a 256-way distribution conditioned on the first pixel. This logic extends by induction: modeling each next pixel in the sequence is a softmax regression problem that models $p(\mathbf{x}_n \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})$. The cross-entropy loss can be computed as shown in (see figure: Autoregressive prediction as next-pixel-classification.).
concepts.motivation_md: By framing image generation as a sequence of classification tasks, we can apply well-understood tools like softmax regression and cross-entropy loss to the complex problem of generative modeling.

concepts.title: Chain Rule of Probability
concepts.one_liner: The chain rule of probability allows any joint distribution to be factorized into a product of conditional distributions.
concepts.content:
The chain rule of probability allows us to factorize any joint distribution into a product of conditionals as follows: 

$$\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{X}) &= p(\mathbf{x_n} \bigm | \mathbf{x_1}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1})p(\mathbf{x}_{n-1} \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-2}) \quad \ldots \quad p(\mathbf{x}_2 \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1)p(\mathbf{x}_1)\\ p(\mathbf{X}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p(\mathbf{x}_i \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{i-1}) \end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Training Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive models are trained using supervised pairs of sequences and their next elements, often using overlapping batches for computational efficiency.
concepts.content:
To train an autoregressive model, you extract supervised pairs of desired input-output behavior. For pixels, this means extracting sequences $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}$ and the corresponding observed next pixel $\mathbf{x}_n$, typically by traversing images in raster order.

(see figure: Training an autoregressive model, then sampling images from it.)

There are two ways to set up training batches. A 'type 1 batch' samples independent [sequence, completion] pairs from random locations in random images. A 'type 2 batch' uses overlapping sequences from the same image: $$\begin{aligned} &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_1^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n-1}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_n^{(i)}\\ &\texttt{input}: \mathbf{x}_2^{(i)}, \dots, \mathbf{x}_{n}^{(i)} \quad\quad \texttt{target output}: \mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{(i)}\\ &\ldots\nonumber \end{aligned}$$ Type 2 batches are much more efficient because representations computed for one prediction can be reused for the next. This is utilized in transformers with causal attention, where the representation of an item only depends on its predecessors, allowing shared computation across overlapping predictions.
concepts.motivation_md: Training on every possible sub-sequence of an image is computationally expensive; type 2 batches allow models like transformers to process multiple prediction targets in a single forward pass.

concepts.title: Sampling from Autoregressive Models
concepts.one_liner: Sampling from an autoregressive model involves sequentially drawing values from conditional categorical distributions.

To sample from this density, we sample the first pixel from $p(\mathbf{x}_1)$, then, conditioned on this, sample the second from $p(\mathbf{x}_2 \bigm | \mathbf{x}_1)$, and so forth. Since each density is a categorical distribution, sampling is straightforward; for example, one can partition a unit line segment into regions proportional to the categorical probabilities and see where a uniform random draw falls. Note that autoregressive models do not have latent variables $\mathbf{z}$, making them incompatible with applications requiring latent variable manipulation.

concepts.title: GAN Minimax Game and Optimization
concepts.one_liner: Generative Adversarial Networks are trained through a minimax game where a generator and discriminator compete to respectively synthesize and detect realistic data.
concepts.content:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) consist of a generator $g_{\theta}$ and a discriminator $d_{\phi}$ that play an adversarial game. The generator $g_{\theta}$ tries to become better at generating synthetic images, while $d_{\phi}$ tries to become better at detecting errors $g_{\theta}$ is making. The learning problem is written as a minimax game:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\theta\max_\phi \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Schematically, the generator synthesizes images that are fed as input to the discriminator. The discriminator tries to assign a high score to generated images (classifying them as synthetic) and a low score to real images from a training set.

(see figure: Architecture of a GAN being trained to generate images of flamingos. The synthetic image in this example is generated by BigGAN @brock2018large)

Although called an adversarial game, the discriminator helps the generator improve by pointing out its current errors. This is analogous to a student (generator) and a teacher (discriminator) in a painting class; the teacher provides feedback on specific errors, such as shading or variety, until the student produces paintings as good as the teacher's. 

From the discriminator's perspective, given a generator $g_{\theta}$, $d_{\phi}$ tries to maximize its ability to discriminate between real and synthetic images. This objective is logistic regression between real data $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and synthetic data $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{(i)})$. The optimal discriminator $d_{\phi}^*$ is defined as:

$$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

From the generator's perspective, given $d_{\phi}^*$, $g_{\theta}$ tries to solve:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}^*(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Because $d_{\phi}^*$ depends on the current $g_{\theta}$, updating the generator requires re-solving for the optimal discriminator. In practice, optimization alternates between taking one gradient step for the generator and $K$ gradient steps for the discriminator (where $K=1$ is often sufficient).
concepts.motivation_md: GANs solve the problem of learning complex, high-dimensional data distributions (like natural images) without requiring a hand-defined loss function. By using a neural network as a learned discriminator, the model can discover and correct subtle statistical discrepancies between real and synthetic data that simple mathematical metrics might miss.

slots.example:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) consist of a generator $g_{\theta}$ and a discriminator $d_{\phi}$ that play an adversarial game. The generator $g_{\theta}$ tries to become better at generating synthetic images, while $d_{\phi}$ tries to become better at detecting errors $g_{\theta}$ is making. The learning problem is written as a minimax game:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_\theta\max_\phi \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Schematically, the generator synthesizes images that are fed as input to the discriminator. The discriminator tries to assign a high score to generated images (classifying them as synthetic) and a low score to real images from a training set.

(see figure: Architecture of a GAN being trained to generate images of flamingos. The synthetic image in this example is generated by BigGAN @brock2018large)

Although called an adversarial game, the discriminator helps the generator improve by pointing out its current errors. This is analogous to a student (generator) and a teacher (discriminator) in a painting class; the teacher provides feedback on specific errors, such as shading or variety, until the student produces paintings as good as the teacher's. 

From the discriminator's perspective, given a generator $g_{\theta}$, $d_{\phi}$ tries to maximize its ability to discriminate between real and synthetic images. This objective is logistic regression between real data $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ and synthetic data $\{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(i)} = g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{(i)})$. The optimal discriminator $d_{\phi}^*$ is defined as:

$$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x} \sim p_{\texttt{data}}}[\log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

From the generator's perspective, given $d_{\phi}^*$, $g_{\theta}$ tries to solve:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z} \sim p_{\mathbf{z}}}[\log (1-d_{\phi}^*(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{z})))] \end{aligned}$$

Because $d_{\phi}^*$ depends on the current $g_{\theta}$, updating the generator requires re-solving for the optimal discriminator. In practice, optimization alternates between taking one gradient step for the generator and $K$ gradient steps for the discriminator (where $K=1$ is often sufficient).

concepts.title: GANs as Statistical Image Models
concepts.one_liner: GANs are learned statistical image models that amortize the optimization process by learning a mapping from latent noise to data samples.
concepts.content: GANs are related to classical image and texture models, such as the Heeger-Bergen model, which synthesize images by matching statistics of a source texture. In such models, optimization adjusts image pixels until specific statistics (like subband histograms) match the training data. In GAN terminology, the loss checking for this match acts as a discriminator. However, unlike GANs, these discriminators are hand-defined rather than learned. Furthermore, GANs amortize the optimization via learning: they learn a mapping $g_{\theta}$ from latent noise to samples, rather than performing a fresh optimization process from scratch for every new sample.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional statistical image models require manually identifying which features (like histograms) are important. GANs improve on this by learning the relevant statistics automatically and providing a fast way to generate new samples through a learned generator function.
concepts.recap_md: - GANs replace hand-defined statistical matches with a learned discriminator network.

prereq.rationale: Sampling is defined as the process of querying a learned generator function to produce outputs.
Sampling involves querying the generator with randomized latent vectors (z-vectors).
The core objective of generative modeling is defined as the creation of a generator function.
Generalization is a secondary property that ensures the model satisfies the generative objective without simply memorizing data.
The direct approach is a specific method for forming the generator function G.
The indirect approach is one strategy for achieving the goal of forming data generators.
The Gaussian distribution is introduced as a specific, fundamental example of a density model.
This technique describes how to estimate the parameters specifically for the Gaussian density model.
A Gaussian mixture model is explicitly defined as a composition of multiple individual Gaussian distributions.
GMMs are presented as a more sophisticated class of density models for representing complex data.
Energy-based models are defined as an alternative to density models that avoids the difficult constraint of a normalized probability density.
The text notes that unnormalized energy functions are sufficient for sampling via MCMC.
The Boltzmann or Gibbs distribution is the specific parametric form used to relate energy functions to normalized densities.
Contrastive divergence is an optimization technique specifically built for energy-based models.
Latent variables are the specific inputs to a generator function that determine the variation in its synthetic output.
Diffusion models are defined as a specific class of generative models that create data by reversing corruption.
The forward diffusion process is the specific signal corruption method that defines the first half of the diffusion model strategy.
The reverse process is trained to undo the specific corruption sequence created by the forward diffusion process.
The reverse diffusion process is implemented by repeatedly applying a trained denoiser network.
Training diffusion models involves fitting the predictor that performs the reverse diffusion mapping.
Density models implement the indirect approach to generative modeling by learning a scoring function (the density) rather than a direct generator mapping.
MCMC is a sampling technique that specifically requires a probability density function as its input to generate samples.
Training involves learning the function that performs the sequential predictions defined by the autoregressive model.
Sampling is the process of generating new data from a trained autoregressive model.
Sampling from an autoregressive model follows the specific order of conditional dependencies defined by the chain rule factorization.
The generator is defined as one of the two primary neural network components that constitute a GAN.
The discriminator is defined as one of the two primary neural network components that constitute a GAN.
The optimization process describes how the constituent parts of a GAN are trained together.
The minimax game involves the generator attempting to synthesize realistic data.
The minimax game involves the discriminator attempting to detect synthetic data.

The indirect approach is defined as an alternative to the direct mapping function used in the direct approach.
EBMs are one of the primary categories of generative models compared in this summary.
Diffusion models are explicitly contrasted with autoregressive models, which remove pixels one by one rather than using signal corruption.
MCMC provides a concrete mechanism for the indirect approach by allowing one to sample from a model that only defines a density.
KL divergence is introduced as a specific, common instance of a divergence measure for comparing distributions.
Autoregressive models are a specific class of density models that provide an explicit density function by decomposing the joint probability into a product of conditionals.
This concept explains the autoregressive process by breaking it down into an inductive sequence of single-pixel predictions.
The text notes that autoregressive models lack latent variables, distinguishing them from other generative architectures like VAEs or GANs.
GANs are described as models that attempt to directly output samples from a complex distribution in one step, fitting the definition of a direct approach.
The GAN generator is a specific neural network implementation of the general generator concept, mapping latent noise to data samples.
